# A uniform rate kernel between surface and inverse-volume defects

This refines the already proved vector flux between surface-log and
inverse-volume defects. Its new conclusion is an exact positive coupling
of their exponential rate distributions, after the legitimate radial
weighting. It is not an identification of their normal or source labels,
and does not imply that either defect vanishes.

Dependencies, with all their explicit positive-fiber hypotheses, are
`candidate d9362f528596f345`,
`candidate 8ba63f3af7e6943f`,
and `candidate 942ae5a91bb1a792`.

## 1. Joint rate limits for the labeled inverse-volume measures

Use their notation. In particular

    ell_j=-log L_j, r_j=lambda_j ell_{j,+},
    nu_ij=(sigma_ij/L_ij)rho_ij,
    sum_i nu_ij=dm_j/(M_j L_j),
    grad_X log L_j dm_j=M_j sum_i c_ij nu_ij.

The finite continuous gradients c_ij converge to c_i. These identities
hold as actual measures, with each nu_ij carried by A_ij=L_j; the current
normal/physical boundary measures are eta_j. All inverse masses are bounded,
the nonnegative rates are uniformly bounded, and L_j converges uniformly.

Adjoin the actual rate coordinate to every nu_ij and take joint weak limits:

    nu_ij delta_(r_j) -> nu_i^0 delta_0 + zetahat_i.       (1)

Here nu_i^0 is the restriction of the ordinary limiting labeled measure
to {L>0}, and zetahat_i is its positive restriction over {L=0}. The ordinary
part has rate zero by boundedness of log L_j away from that zero set. Labels
with sigma_i=0 vanish by the marked-value lower bound. Each zetahat_i is
supported on A_i=L=0 and has rates in [0,beta]. Its rate projection is
exactly the previously retained zeta_i. There is no added uniform
integrability assumption for 1/L_j.

Let bhat be the surface defect with rate retained, so

    ell_{j,+} eta_j delta_(r_j)
       -> ell_+ eta delta_0 + bhat.                     (2)

The contact-row limit theorem separately proves uniform integrability of
the BULK logarithms. That fact, unlike reciprocal uniform integrability,
is available and will be used below.

## 2. Rate-weighted vector flux

For every continuously differentiable g on a neighborhood of [0,beta],
with a harmless extension to the common prelimit rate interval, define

    F_j=ell_{j,+} g(r_j).

For each fixed j this is Lipschitz on the current body. Its weak continuous
gradient is

    grad_X F_j
      =-1_(L_j<1)[g(r_j)+r_j g'(r_j)] grad_X log L_j.  (3)

The positive-part function is continuous, so no interface measure occurs
on L_j=1. The same is true at a crease of finite-PL L_j.

For a scalar test phi that is C1 in the continuous variables at each finite
base, Gauss--Green gives

    integral phi F_j n d eta_j
      =integral F_j grad_X phi dm_j
        -M_j sum_i c_ij integral phi 1_(L_j<1)
                          [g(r_j)+r_j g'(r_j)] d nu_ij. (4)

The boundary term converges by (2). The bulk F_j term converges to
g(0) integral ell_+ grad_X phi dm. Indeed the rates tend to zero locally
where L>0, g is bounded on the compact rate range, and bulk-log uniform
integrability permits passage across the small-L region.

The possible discontinuity of 1_(L_j<1) in the last term deserves care.
One can first use smooth cutoffs in ell_j which agree with its positive
part outside |ell_j|<delta, pass to the limit, and then let delta decrease.
Alternatively use the following direct observation. The gradient vector
measure on a limiting fiber with L=1 on a positive-volume subset is zero
there: each active continuous gradient is zero on that subset. Where
L=1 is volume-null the cutoff passes by bounded local densities. On the
defect support L=0 the cutoff is identically one for all sufficiently
large j in each fixed sufficiently small neighborhood. Thus the limiting
last term is its ordinary weak-gradient contribution plus

    -M sum_i c_i integral phi [g(r)+r g'(r)] d zetahat_i.

Subtract the limiting-body Gauss--Green identity for g(0)ell_+. We obtain
the exact rate-weighted vector identity

    - integral phi(w)n g(r) d bhat(n,w,r)
       =M sum_i c_i integral phi(w)[g(r)+r g'(r)]
                                                   d zetahat_i(w,r). (5)

An entirely simpler rigorous way to avoid the cutoff detail is to prove
(5) first for g(r)=r^m. For m>=1, both the limiting ordinary term and the
coefficient at rate zero vanish. At L_j near one the coefficient r_j^m
vanishes uniformly, so there is no cutoff issue. For m=0, (5) is exactly
the already proved unweighted defect-flux theorem. Linear combinations
give all polynomials; approximation of g and g' uniformly on the compact
rate interval gives (5) for C1 functions. This is the proof used for the
consequences below; no cutoff claim is necessary for them.

In particular, for every integer m>=0,

    - integral phi n r^m d bhat
       =M(m+1) sum_i c_i integral phi r^m d zetahat_i.   (6)

Physical test density extends (5)--(6) to continuous phi. Neither formula
allows a freely chosen normal argument on its right, or splits bhat into
positive source-labeled surface measures.

## 3. A positive radial identity at every rate moment

Choose fixed inball centers g_z, with common radius r_b>0, as in the
unweighted flux theorem. Write

    h(n,z,X)=n.(X-g_z)>0

on the actual limiting defect normal bundle. On zetahat_i the affine
contact relation A_i(z,X)=0 gives

    c_i.(X-g_z)=-A_i(z,g_z),

where A_i(z,g_z) is uniformly positive and bounded. Dot (6) with the
continuous vector field X-g_z, and retain an arbitrary continuous physical
scalar multiplier phi. This proves

    integral phi(w) h(n,w) r^m d bhat
       =M(m+1) sum_i integral phi(w) A_i(z,g_z) r^m
                                                   d zetahat_i. (7)

Define POSITIVE measures on physical-position/rate space by

    B=pi_(w,r)*(h bhat),
    V=M sum_i A_i(z,g_z) zetahat_i,                      (8)

where the projection forgets only the boundary normal. Equation (7) says

    integral phi(w) r^m dV
       =1/(m+1) integral phi(w) r^m dB.                (9)

The independent choices of g_z are permitted: Gauss--Green is performed
fiberwise. No claim is made that their graph is globally affine or that
h is a permitted physical convex test. Its role here is the exact flux,
not the separator inequality.

## 4. Exact uniform-kernel representation

For R>0 let U_R be uniform probability measure on [0,R]; put U_0=delta_0.
Construct a positive measure by keeping the physical point fixed and
applying this kernel to B:

    Vtilde(dw,ds)=integral_(R in [0,beta])
                                      U_R(ds) B(dw,dR). (10)

Its m-th rate moment at each continuous physical test is precisely the
right side of (9), since integral s^m dU_R=R^m/(m+1), including R=0
and m=0. Thus V and Vtilde agree against every product phi(w)r^m.
Polynomial approximation on the compact rate interval and finite sums of
product continuous functions on the compact physical/rate product imply
equality of the measures. We have proved

    V(dw,ds)=integral U_R(ds) B(dw,dR).                  (11)

This is a deterministic measure identity, not a randomized selection of
an OC center. In particular its rate projection has an atom at zero of
mass B(rate=0), and on (0,beta] it is absolutely continuous with density

    s -> integral_(R>=s) (1/R) B(dR),                  (12)

up to irrelevant choices at endpoints. The density is nonincreasing.
Formula (11), rather than an unweighted claim about zeta, is the precise
positive relation: V has the essential source-plane weights and B the
essential radial support weights from (8).

It follows also that positive-rate inverse defect cannot have an atom at
any fixed positive rate. Each source-plane weight in (8) is bounded below,
so each individual zetahat_i inherits this absence of positive-rate atoms.
There may still be arbitrary tangential physical concentration and a rate
zero atom. No exclusion of b, zeta, or the original boundary concentration
is proved by (11).
